title: New Year's death remains a mystery to family
article: Several months after Ryan Snopek died, his family is still looking for an official explanation around the events that led to his death in RCMP custody.
The 30-year-old man was allegedly intoxicated and causing a disturbance when he was arrested at a private residence in Cranbrook on New Year's Eve.
The next morning, a jail guard noticed Mr. Snopek was unconscious, and he was taken to hospital where he was declared dead.
Joe Snopek, the man's uncle, said the family has received very little information since the incident more than nine months ago.
A few days after the death, the family was told that the victim suffered a brain hemorrhage as a result of a skull fracture suffered from a fall.
"Since then, absolutely nothing," said the uncle, who is the mayor of the town of Creston.

There have been conflicting and unconfirmed reports about whether the man had already passed out when he was arrested by police and put into a cell. It is not known when he suffered the injury that led to his death.

A coroner's inquest is mandatory in British Columbia when there is a death in police custody. The inquest will take place next spring, although an exact date has not yet been finalized, a spokesman for the B.C. Coroners Service said yesterday.
The family is frustrated by the slow pace of the process, Mr. Snopek said, as an inquest may be the only way to find out how Ryan died.
"I would like to know how police deal with someone before they are thrown into a drunk tank," Mr. Snopek said. "One of the problems is we have the RCMP looking into the RCMP."
The RCMP major crimes unit in Kelowna conducted the criminal investigation into the incident, which involved officers at its Cranbrook/Kimberley detachment.
A report to Crown counsel was initially submitted to the Ministry of the Attorney-General in April.

The Crown decided last month that there were no grounds to file criminal charges. The "charge assessment" was in relation to "earlier events," before the dead man was arrested, said Stan Lowe, a spokesman for Crown counsel in B.C.
He stressed that medical evidence "eliminated any occurrences while in custody" as a cause of death, and police officers were not the subject of the criminal investigation.
Mr. Lowe said he sympathized with the Snopek family over the lengthiness of the process but suggested that "everything will come out" at the coroner's inquest.
A civilian review of the conduct of the officers is on hold, however, after a formal complaint was unilaterally terminated by the RCMP.
The B.C. Civil Liberties Association asked the Commission for Public Complaints Against the RCMP to review the death because it happened while the victim was in police custody.

The senior officer at the Cranbrook/Kimberley detachment notified the civil liberties group in August that the RCMP was terminating the complaint filed with its civilian oversight agency by invoking powers contained in a section of the RCMP Act.
"This termination is not an attempt to avoid accountability but a desire to avoid unnecessary multiplicity of proceedings," Staff Sergeant B.R.R. Edmondson wrote.
The RCMP letter noted that the matter was already being reviewed by the Crown and that there would be a coroner's inquest, so an inquiry by its oversight agency was not necessary.
The civil liberties group has since asked the chair of the public complaints commission to review the RCMP's decision to terminate the complaint.
